nameStory: The 'folding-door' spider gets its name from its remarkable burrow design - it creates a hinged trapdoor that folds open and shut like a cabinet door! Unlike their trapdoor spider cousins who make doors that lift straight up, these clever architects engineer doors that swing on a hinge. The 'unicolor' part of their scientific name means 'one color,' reflecting their fairly uniform dark coloration.
description: The Folding-door Spider is a stocky, dark-colored spider that lives most of its life hidden in underground burrows. These spiders are typically dark brown to nearly black with a robust, compact body that looks almost furry due to fine hairs covering their surface. They're medium-sized spiders, though exact measurements vary, with thick legs built for digging rather than running. What makes them truly special is their engineering skill - they construct silk-lined burrows topped with hinged doors that blend perfectly with the surrounding ground.

idTips.label: Burrow Door
idTips.description: Look for a hinged trapdoor flush with the ground that swings open on one side like a tiny cabinet door, often covered with bits of soil and debris that make it nearly invisible

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, compact spider with a velvety texture from dense, short hairs covering the dark brown to black body

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Thick, powerful legs that feel sturdy rather than delicate, with the front legs often appearing slightly more robust for digging

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely secretive, rarely seen above ground except at night; when disturbed, they retreat quickly into their burrow and pull the door shut

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized spider that feels substantial when handled, with a body that appears almost cube-like rather than elongated

habitat: Folding-door Spiders prefer well-drained soils in wooded areas where they can excavate their burrows without hitting water or rocky substrates. In New England, look for them in deciduous and mixed forests with loose, organic-rich soil, often on gentle slopes or level ground. Their burrows are typically found in areas with some leaf litter that helps camouflage their trapdoors.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as soil warms, and this is when you're most likely to spot them outside their burrows during evening hours or after rain.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when mating occurs and females may be found with egg sacs in their burrows. Males occasionally wander above ground searching for mates.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare burrows for winter, reinforcing doors and deepening chambers. Young spiders may disperse to establish new territories.
seasonality.winter: Completely inactive, sealed deep in their silk-lined burrows below the frost line, with doors firmly shut until spring warmth returns.

funFact: These spiders are living fossils - their family has been using the same trapdoor technology for over 100 million years, meaning they were already master engineers when T-Rex roamed the Earth!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other trapdoor spiders, but folding-door spiders have doors that swing sideways on hinges rather than lifting straight up like a manhole cover. If you can gently lift the door and it pivots to one side, you've found a folding-door spider!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'folding-door spiders,' they're often grouped with trapdoor spiders in casual conversation, though they belong to a completely different family with their own unique door-building technique. This is one of the rarest spider encounters you can have in New England, with only a handful of confirmed sightings.
compareHints: Since this is the only Antrodiaetus species recorded in New England, compare it to other trapdoor-style spiders by focusing on the door mechanism - folding-door spiders' doors swing on hinges rather than lift up. The burrow construction and door-hinging behavior is the key distinguishing feature from all other burrowing spiders in the region.
